issues.item: Triggers: Sexual Trauma Cues: Comments on sexual violence
issues.explanation: 'Comments on sexual violence' is hard to reconcile with a primary trauma of life-threatening accident in the absence of any sexual-trauma content elsewhere in triggers, memory, threat, or appraisals. This is not just unusual; it suggests a different trauma theme than the stated index event.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Prevention Rumination: I dwell on how the event could have been prevented
issues.explanation: 'I dwell on how the event could have been prevented' can occur after accidents, but here the rest of the profile centers on sensory trauma cues and intrusive memory/avoidance rather than a coherent prevention-focused appraisal pattern. With Negative Appraisals absent and no threat/appraisal content linking to preventability, this strategy feels weakly grounded relative to the formulation and selected items.

vignette:
Javier Morales, a 62-year-old Latin American man, had spent most of his adult life working as a surgeon, a role that had trained him to stay composed in the face of blood, urgency, and other people’s fear. Until the accident, he had assumed that experience had made him steady in ways that would hold up outside the hospital as well. The trauma occurred years into his career, when a routine drive home ended in a violent collision that left him pinned in a wrecked car after another vehicle struck his at speed. What stayed with him most was not only the shock of impact, but the sickening tactile detail of it: the harsh, unfamiliar texture of twisted metal and torn upholstery pressing against his hands as he struggled to orient himself. Even now, that texture seemed to have a strange power over him; if his fingers brushed against something rough, frayed, or sharply ridged in just the wrong way, he could feel a jolt of recognition that seemed to pull him back into the crushed interior of the car. In the months that followed, Javier found that certain images arrived with almost intrusive force, especially the sight of cars hit by accident. Passing a crumpled vehicle on the roadside or seeing a damaged car in a parking lot could seize his attention so completely that he felt temporarily unable to look anywhere else.

From the beginning, the memory of the event had not felt like an ordinary recollection to him. Javier described it as more real than normal, vivid in a way that made other memories seem faded and distant by comparison. He could recall not just the sequence of events, but the angle of light, the pressure in his chest, the smell inside the car, and the abrupt terror of realizing he was trapped. Yet when he tried to think through the whole incident calmly, he often found himself pushing the memory away before he could fully recall it. He would sense the first few seconds of the crash, then stop himself, as if there were a limit to how much of it he could safely let into awareness. At other times, the memory forced its way into his mind when he did not want it there. This happened without warning while he was speaking with colleagues, waiting in line, or sitting quietly at home with his wife. He would abruptly find himself back in the wreck, alert to the same helplessness he had felt then, his attention narrowed around the event despite his effort to remain in the present.

As the years passed, Javier began shaping his life around the possibility of being pulled back into that state. He gave up pleasant activities that had once made weekends feel restorative, gradually declining dinners out, drives with his wife, and small trips that involved time in a car. He told himself that these choices were practical and not worth dwelling on, but he also knew he was avoiding the risk of hearing, seeing, or even smelling something that might bring the accident to mind. He also avoided physical stress. Activities that put his body under strain became increasingly difficult to justify, and he steered himself toward routines that felt controlled and low-risk. In a profession that already demanded long hours and physical endurance, this was not easy to sustain. At work, he remained functional, but he became more selective about anything that required him to push his body or move quickly for extended periods. He noticed that these decisions narrowed his life in quiet but consequential ways. His wife urged him to join her in things they had once enjoyed together, but he often declined, and over time she had come to see him as less present, more cautious, and harder to persuade.

Javier did not speak readily about the accident, and he worked hard to avoid thinking about it in any deliberate way. He preferred to keep his mind occupied with tasks, cases, and practical responsibilities, because once he allowed himself to linger on the event, he feared it would become harder to shut out. Yet the effort to keep away from the memory was increasingly difficult. The sight of a damaged car on his commute, a conversation about traffic injuries, or the simple feel of a particular rough surface could make the event seem immediately close again. He was especially unsettled by how suddenly the memory could intrude, as if his mind no longer respected the boundary between the past and the present. Although he remained a surgeon with a reputation for competence, privately he had grown less willing to trust the ease with which he once moved through the world. By the time he sought help, he was exhausted by the amount of energy it took to manage his reactions and by the sense that he had gradually organized his life around what he could no longer bear to revisit. What finally brought Javier into treatment was the realization that he was losing too much of the life he had built with his wife, while also feeling increasingly vulnerable to the memory that would not stay put. More than anything, he hoped to be able to think about the accident without being overwhelmed by its vividness, and to reclaim parts of ordinary life without constantly bracing himself for the next unwanted return of the crash.
